findings.original: it is the mode in which they gained a livelihood that explains why here politics, and there Catholicism, played the chief part.
findings.rewrite: it is the way in which they earned their living that explains why politics played the chief part in the one case, and Catholicism in the other.
findings.problem: The preceding sentence names the middle ages first, so "the one case" now reads as the middle ages and the rewrite pairs politics with the middle ages and Catholicism with the ancient world. That reverses Marx's pairing: politics goes with Athens and Rome, Catholicism with the middle ages.
findings.fix: it is the way in which they earned their living that explains why politics played the chief part in the ancient world, and Catholicism in the middle ages.

findings.original: Moderate though he be, yet some few wants he has to satisfy
findings.rewrite: Modest though he is, he still has a few wants to satisfy
findings.problem: Here "moderate" means frugal or content with little, which is the point about his few wants. "Modest" most often means humble, so it shifts the trait being described.
findings.fix: Frugal though he is, he still has a few wants to satisfy

findings.original: Tagwerk, Tagwanne (jurnale, or terra jurnalis, or diornalis), Mannsmaad, &c.
findings.problem: The gloss is a guess from "Wanne" (winnowing basket). Tagwan/Tagwen is an old variant of Tagwerk meaning a day's work, so the bracketed translation probably mistranslates the word. §2.3 requires a literal and accurate translation.

findings.original: The economic discoverers of this chemical element, who by-the-bye lay special claim to critical acumen, find however that the use value of objects belongs to them independently of their material properties, while their value, on the other hand, forms a part of them as objects.
findings.rewrite: The economic discoverers of this chemical element, who, by the way, lay special claim to critical sharpness, find, however, that the use-value of objects belongs to them independently of their material properties, while their value, on the other hand, forms a part of them as objects.
findings.problem: Sentences across the unit average about 26 words, above the 15–22 target, and a dozen still run past 45 words (for example p132, p136 twice, p139, p143, p144, p145 twice, and this one plus the next sentence in p152).
findings.fix: Split it: "The economic discoverers of this chemical element, by the way, lay special claim to critical sharpness. They find, however, that the use-value of objects belongs to them independently of their material properties, while their value, on the other hand, forms a part of them as objects." Split the other 45+-word sentences listed at natural breaks in the same way, without moving any qualifier or the deliberately ambiguous "therefore" in p136.

findings.original: It not only stands with its feet on the ground, but, in relation to all other commodities, it stands on its head
findings.rewrite: It not only stands with its feet on the ground. In relation to all other commodities, it also stands on its head
findings.problem: Splitting at "not only" leaves a sentence that is incomplete without its "but" and weakens the contrast between the two images.
findings.fix: It not only stands with its feet on the ground, but, in relation to all other commodities, it also stands on its head

findings.original: What are we to think of a law that asserts itself only by periodical revolutions?
findings.rewrite: What are we to think of a law that asserts itself only through periodical revolutions?
findings.problem: Engels's quotation is already readable. §2.2 says it should then stay word for word, so the change from "by" to "through" is not allowed.
findings.fix: What are we to think of a law that asserts itself only by periodical revolutions?

findings.original: A ridiculous presumption has latterly got abroad that common property in its primitive form is specifically a Slavonian, or even exclusively Russian form.
findings.rewrite: A ridiculous assumption has lately spread that common property in its primitive form is a specifically Slavic, or even an exclusively Russian, form.
findings.problem: This is a quotation from "Zur Kritik", just like n. 30, yet n. 30 is kept verbatim with British spelling while this one is reworded throughout (presumption, Slavonian, amongst, exhaustive, deducible, reordered clauses). That goes beyond §2.2 and treats the two quotations inconsistently.
findings.fix: Restore the note's quoted text near-verbatim, as in n. 30. Change only the archaic "latterly got abroad" (for example to "lately spread"), and keep "presumption", "Slavonian", "amongst", "exhaustive", "deducible" and the original clause order.

notes_review: Most logged calls are sound. They include: no §7 gloss for Fetishism, where Marx defines it himself; the §7 gloss for circulation in p139; the preserved ambiguities in p136, p138 and p152; leaving the stray closing quotation mark in n. 31; "exchange rate" for "course of exchange"; and the neutral Dogberry, Physiocrats, tithe and suzerains identifications. Three calls do not hold up. The "Tagwanne" gloss is a guess and probably wrong. Note 16's claim that "in the one case… in the other" keeps the same order is mistaken, because the phrase flips the referents. The n. 32 gloss on classical political economy is defensible but borderline, since Marx gives his own definition in n. 33 of the same paragraph. The 1.02 length ratio is acceptable: I confirmed that the quotations (nn. 30, 32, 34, p151) are verbatim and that no content was dropped.
summary: Fidelity is high. Every claim, number, citation, foreign text, attribution and ironic tag (our friend Robinson, Mr. Sedley Taylor, the speaking commodities, Bastiat the dwarf economist) survives, and the one real meaning error is the reversed politics/Catholicism pairing in n. 34. Readability is acceptable but still dense: average sentence length is about 26 words, so the longest remaining sentences should be split further.
